joint-grid.t: Here is the **joint table** of bedrooms (X, rows) and price band (Y, columns). From this one table we can answer **two different kinds of questions**.

marginalize-y.h: MARGINAL: ADD ACROSS THE OTHER VARIABLE
marginalize-y.t: To study bedrooms alone, **ignore the price**: add each row across the Low and High columns. We are collapsing the Y axis.

x-marginal.t: The row totals are the **marginal distribution**: **P(X = 1) = 0.30, P(X = 2) = 0.40, P(X = 3) = 0.30**. They add up to 1. This is bedrooms over **all** houses.

select-y.h: CONDITIONAL: WE LEARN THAT Y = HIGH
select-y.t: Now suppose we are told the house is **High priced**. Low priced houses are no longer possible, so we **keep only the High column** and drop the rest.

conditional-slice.t: The slice holds **0.05, 0.20 and 0.25**. These are probabilities out of **all** houses, and they add up to **0.50, not 1**. It is not yet a distribution.

normalize.t: Divide each entry by the slice total **0.50**: **0.10, 0.40, 0.50**. Now they add up to 1. This is the **conditional distribution P(X | Y = High)**.

compare.t: Marginal: **0.30, 0.40, 0.30** (all houses). Conditional on High: **0.10, 0.40, 0.50**. Knowing the price **shifted the probability toward bigger houses**.

ml-connection.t: A **marginal** describes one feature on its own. **Prediction is conditioning**: observe some variables, then ask about the others, always renormalizing. The multivariate normal later does exactly this.
